mainTopic: Whether קנין פירות is like קנין הגוף: the dispute of רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש, why it is recorded twice, and the challenge from a chain of recipients ('after you')
overview: This amud continues the case of a father who wrote his property to his son but kept the right to its fruits for life. The son sold the land and then died before his father. רבי יוחנן says the buyer did not acquire it, and ריש לקיש says he did. Their disagreement is whether קנין פירות (owning the fruits) counts like קנין הגוף (owning the land itself). The גמרא asks why they needed to argue twice, since they already disagreed about someone who sold only the fruits of his field and whether the buyer reads the ביכורים verses. It answers that each side needed the father-and-son case to block a different mistaken idea. Then רבי יוחנן challenges ריש לקיש from a ברייתא about a chain of recipients: 'my property to you, and after you to so-and-so.' ריש לקיש answers that the wording 'after you' is different, as רב הושעיא and רב already said. Finally, the גמרא quotes a second ברייתא that rules the opposite way, and the discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Did the buyer acquire the land?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן rules the buyer did not acquire. ריש לקיש rules the buyer did acquire.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן says: The buyer did not acquire. And ריש לקיש says: The buyer acquired.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a disagreement about the case under discussion: the son sold land his father had given him, and the son died while the father was still alive.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The son owned the land itself, but his father still had the right to its fruits. The question is whether the son's sale holds once the son dies before the father. רבי יוחנן says the sale fails, and ריש לקיש says it stands.

keyTerms.meaning: רבי שמעון בן לקיש, the regular partner and disputant of רבי יוחנן

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: לֹא קָנָה לוֹקֵחַ.
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan says: The buyer did not acquire.
phrases.notes: This is the buyer who bought the land from the son, who then died before his father.

phrases.english: And Reish Lakish says: The buyer acquired.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: לֹא קָנָה לוֹקֵחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the dispute about the son's sale.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יוחנן: the sale fails. ריש לקיש: the sale is valid.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן's reason: owning the fruits is like owning the land
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן holds קנין פירות כקנין הגוף דמי, so the father counts as the owner and the son's sale never took effect.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן says the buyer did not acquire, because ownership of the fruits is like ownership of the thing itself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the reasoning behind רבי יוחנן's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the father has all the fruits, רבי יוחנן treats him as if he owns the land itself. So the son had nothing he could sell yet. Because the son died before the father, he never became the full owner, and the sale never takes effect.

keyTerms.meaning: ownership of the fruits or profits of something (the right to use it)

steps.whyThisMatters: This principle, קנין פירות כקנין הגוף, is a major idea that shows up in many places in ש״ס.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר: לֹא קָנָה לוֹקֵחַ –
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan says: The buyer did not acquire,
because ownership of the fruits is like ownership of the thing itself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason for רבי יוחנן's ruling in step 1.

steps.title: ריש לקיש's reason: owning the fruits is not like owning the land
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש holds קנין פירות לאו כקנין הגוף דמי, so the son, who owns the land itself, could sell it.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש says the buyer acquired, because ownership of the fruits is not like ownership of the thing itself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the reasoning behind ריש לקיש's opposite ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For ריש לקיש, the father's right to the fruits does not make him the owner of the land. The son truly owned the land, so his sale works. The buyer gets the land fully once the father dies.
steps.whatToRemember: The whole disagreement comes down to one question: does owning the fruits count as owning the land? רבי יוחנן says yes, and ריש לקיש says no.

phrases.english: And Reish Lakish says: The buyer acquired,

phrases.aramaic: קִנְיַן פֵּירוֹת לָאו כְּקִנְיַן הַגּוּף דָּמֵי.
phrases.english: because ownership of the fruits is not like ownership of the thing itself.

steps.triggerLanguage: קִנְיַן פֵּירוֹת לָאו כְּקִנְיַן הַגּוּף דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite reasoning, for ריש לקיש's ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: קנין פירות לאו כקנין הגוף דמי.

steps.title: Didn't they already argue about this?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: this same disagreement between רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש was already recorded once, so why repeat it?
steps.simpleTranslation: But they already argued about this one time!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא objects that this dispute looks like a repeat of an argument these two אמוראים already had. It is about to show where that earlier argument appears.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge is not against either opinion. It is about why the dispute is recorded twice. If the same principle was already argued, a second record seems unneeded.

keyTerms.meaning: but surely; an opening word for a challenge

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying either side is wrong. It is only asking why the same argument appears twice.

phrases.english: But they already argued about this one time!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for the dispute just explained.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need to record the dispute of רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש in this case.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same principle, whether קנין פירות is like קנין הגוף, was already argued by them elsewhere, so this looks repetitive.

steps.title: The earlier argument: selling the fruits of a field and ביכורים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the earlier dispute. If someone sells only the fruits of his field, רבי יוחנן says the buyer brings ביכורים and reads the verses, and ריש לקיש says he brings them but does not read.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was stated: One who sells his field for its fruits: רבי יוחנן says he brings first fruits and reads the verses. And ריש לקיש says he brings but does not read.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up its challenge by quoting the earlier argument, which depends on the same principle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When bringing ביכורים, one says the verse about 'the land You gave me', which fits only a person who owns the land. רבי יוחנן lets the buyer of the fruits read it, since owning the fruits is like owning the land. ריש לקיש says he may not read it, because he does not own the land, so this is the same disagreement as before.

keyTerms.meaning: as it was stated (quoting a teaching of the אמוראים)
one who sells his field only for its fruits

steps.whatToRemember: Both cases depend on the same question about קנין פירות. That is why the גמרא asks why the dispute had to be recorded twice.

phrases.english: As it was stated: One who sells his field for its fruits,
phrases.notes: He keeps the land itself and sells only the right to its produce.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan says: He brings and reads.
phrases.notes: The buyer brings ביכורים and reads the verses, which include 'the land You gave me' (דברים 26:10).

phrases.aramaic: וְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אָמַר: מֵבִיא, וְאֵינוֹ קוֹרֵא.
phrases.english: And Reish Lakish says: He brings, but does not read.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source showing the challenge in step 4 is real.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש already argued about whether קנין פירות is like קנין הגוף.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The recorded dispute about a buyer of a field's fruits and whether he reads the ביכורים verses.

steps.title: The earlier dispute rests on the very same principle
steps.stepSummary: The ביכורים dispute is explained with the same reasons: רבי יוחנן holds קנין פירות כקנין הגוף דמי, and ריש לקיש holds it is not. So why say the dispute twice?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן says the buyer brings ביכורים and reads, because he holds that owning the fruits is like owning the land itself. ריש לקיש says he brings but does not read, because owning the fruits is not like owning the land itself. So this is the same argument again!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its challenge from step 4. It shows that the ביכורים dispute is built on exactly the same idea as our case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ביכורים case, the buyer owns only the fruits. Whether he can read 'the land You gave me' depends on whether owning fruits counts as owning the land. That is the same question as in our case, so the repetition looks unnecessary.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said: he brings and reads,

phrases.aramaic: קָסָבַר: קִנְיַן פֵּירוֹת כְּקִנְיַן הַגּוּף דָּמֵי.
phrases.english: because he holds: owning the fruits is like owning the thing itself.

phrases.aramaic: וְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אָמַר: מֵבִיא וְאֵינוֹ קוֹרֵא –
phrases.english: And Reish Lakish said: he brings but does not read,

phrases.aramaic: קִנְיַן פֵּירוֹת לָאו כְּקִנְיַן הַגּוּף דָּמֵי!
phrases.english: because owning the fruits is not like owning the thing itself!

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אָמַר מֵבִיא וְקוֹרֵא קָסָבַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the quote from step 5 by giving each side's reason, which sharpens the challenge of step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need to record the dispute of רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש in our case
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both disputes come down to whether קנין פירות counts as קנין הגוף, so one of them seems unnecessary.

steps.title: Why רבי יוחנן needed the father-and-son case
steps.stepSummary: Even though רבי יוחנן holds קנין פירות כקנין הגוף in general, he needed our case. Otherwise we might think a father gives up his rights for his son.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן can tell you: even though in general owning the fruits is like owning the land, here it was needed. You might have thought a father gives up his rights in favor of his son. He teaches us that he does not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from רבי יוחנן's side. It shows the father-and-son case teaches something new for him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might think a father who kept the fruits would happily let his son control the land, so the son's sale should work. רבי יוחנן teaches that even here, the father's fruit ownership still counts as owning the land, so the sale fails.

keyTerms.meaning: He fully gave up his rights
It teaches us (that this is not so)

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan can say to you:
even though in general
owning the fruits is like owning the thing itself,
here it was needed;
it might enter your mind to say:
a father, toward his son, gives up his rights,
so it teaches us otherwise.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָךְ רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן אַף עַל גַּב דִּבְעָלְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 6 for רבי יוחנן's side.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing a new point (צריכותא): the second case blocks a possible mistake
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A father gives up his rights for his son, so the son's sale would work.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even between father and son, the father's קנין פירות counts as owning the land, so the son's sale fails.

steps.title: Why ריש לקיש needed the father-and-son case
steps.stepSummary: Even though ריש לקיש holds קנין פירות is not like קנין הגוף in general, he needed our case. Otherwise we might think a person always keeps the better share for himself, even against his son.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש says: even though in general owning the fruits is not like owning the land, here it was needed. You might have thought that a person always puts himself first, even ahead of his son. He teaches us that this is not so.
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא answers the challenge from ריש לקיש's side. It shows the father-and-son case teaches something new for him too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might think the father, looking out for himself, really kept the land too, not just the fruits, so the son could not sell. ריש לקיש teaches that the father kept only the fruits, so the son owned the land and his sale works.

keyTerms.meaning: Even when his son is involved
He prefers himself / puts himself first

steps.whatToRemember: Each side recorded the father-and-son case to block a different wrong idea: for רבי יוחנן, that the father gives in to his son; for ריש לקיש, that the father keeps everything for himself.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish can say:
phrases.notes: This is the full name of ריש לקיש.

phrases.english: even though in general

phrases.aramaic: קִנְיַן פֵּירוֹת לָאו כְּקִנְיַן הַגּוּף דָּמֵי,
phrases.english: owning the fruits is not like owning the thing itself,
here it was needed;
it might enter your mind to say:
anyone, when it comes to himself,
even where his son is concerned,
prefers himself;
phrases.notes: So you might think the father kept the land itself too, and the son had nothing to sell.

phrases.english: so it teaches us otherwise.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ אָמַר אַף עַל גַּב דִּבְעָלְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallel answer to step 7, now for ריש לקיש's side.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing a new point (צריכותא): the second case blocks a possible mistake
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A person puts himself first even against his son, so the father kept the land too and the son's sale fails.
steps.terutzMaskana: The father kept only the fruits, which do not count as owning the land, so the son's sale works.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן objects from a chain of inheritors
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן brings a ברייתא against ריש לקיש: if someone says 'my property to you, after you to so-and-so, and after him to so-and-so,' each next person gets it when the one before him dies.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן challenged ריש לקיש from a ברייתא: 'My property is yours, after you so-and-so inherits, and after him so-and-so inherits.' When the first dies, the second gets it. When the second dies, the third gets it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן starts an objection against ריש לקיש by quoting a ברייתא. Here the גמרא is only setting up the case; how it attacks ריש לקיש comes in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא describes property passed down a line of people, one after another. The new information is the ruling that the property moves from first to second to third as each one dies. The גמרא will next use this to challenge ריש לקיש's view.

keyTerms.meaning: He challenged him (from an outside source)

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan raised an objection to Reish Lakish:
"My property is yours,
and after you, so-and-so will inherit,
and after him, so-and-so will inherit" —
if the first dies, the second acquires it.
If the second dies, the third acquires it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After settling why the dispute was repeated, the גמרא moves to a new challenge against ריש לקיש.
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's view that קנין פירות is not like קנין הגוף
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא rules that the property passes to the second and third in turn; the גמרא is about to show how this ruling clashes with ריש לקיש.

steps.title: The ending of the ברייתא and the challenge to ריש לקיש
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says that if the second person dies while the first is still alive, the property goes to the first person's heirs. רבי יוחנן argues that if ריש לקיש were right, it should go to the giver's heirs.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the second person died while the first was still alive, the property goes to the heirs of the first. And if ריש לקיש is right, the ברייתא should have said it goes to the heirs of the giver!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן finishes quoting the ברייתא from step 9 and shows why its ruling is a problem for ריש לקיש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first person only received the property 'until it passes to the next one,' so ריש לקיש would say he only had the fruits. If owning the fruits is not owning the field, the field itself never left the giver. Then, once the chain breaks, it should go back to the giver's heirs and not to the first person's heirs.

keyTerms.meaning: The heirs of the first person who received the gift
The giver, the original owner who handed out the gift
'And if it is so', meaning 'if your view were correct'

steps.confusionAlert: The first line is not a new source. It is the end of the same ברייתא that began in step 9. The challenge comes only in the words וְאִם אִיתָא.

phrases.english: If the second died during the lifetime of the first,
the property goes back to the heirs of the first.
And if it is so,
phrases.notes: He means: if ריש לקיש is right that owning the fruits is not owning the field.

phrases.english: it should have said: to the heirs of the giver!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם אִיתָא, לְיוֹרְשֵׁי נוֹתֵן מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא quoted in step 9 and draws the challenge from it
steps.kashyaTarget: ריש לקיש's view that קנין פירות לאו כקנין הגוף דמי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Since the property goes to the first person's heirs, the first person must have owned the field itself, even though he was only given the property until the next person's turn. If owning the fruits did not count as owning the field, the giver's heirs should get it.

steps.title: ריש לקיש answers that the wording 'after you' is different
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש answers that רב הושעיא already explained that a gift worded 'after you' is a special case. רב gave the same answer when רבה בר רב הונא raised this question.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said to רבי יוחנן: רב הושעיא already explained this in בבל. 'After you' is different. And רבה בר רב הונא also raised this contradiction before רב, and רב said: 'After you' is different.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש defends his view by saying the ברייתא is talking about a special wording, 'after you.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש does not give up his general rule. He says that when a giver says 'my property is yours, and after you to so-and-so,' he really meant to give the first person full ownership of the field itself. That is why the property goes to the first person's heirs, so the ברייתא proves nothing about ordinary fruit ownership.

keyTerms.meaning: He explained it, meaning he interpreted the ברייתא
'After you', the wording of the gift
'Is different', meaning it is a special case

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a key idea: the exact wording of a gift can show that the giver meant to transfer the field itself, not just its fruits.

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: ריש לקיש is answering רבי יוחנן.

phrases.english: Rav Hoshaya already explained it in Babylonia:
'After you' is different.

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן רָמֵי רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא
phrases.english: And so too, Rabba bar Rav Huna raised this contradiction
before Rav, and he said:
'After you' is different.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּבָר תַּרְגְּמַהּ רַב הוֹשַׁעְיָא בְּבָבֶל: ״אַחֲרֶיךָ״ שָׁאנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 10 by limiting the ברייתא to a special wording
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case: the ברייתא deals with a special wording that gives full ownership
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא shows that ordinary fruit ownership counts as owning the field itself
steps.terutzMaskana: The wording 'after you' means the giver gave the first person the field itself, so the ruling does not touch ריש לקיש's general rule

steps.title: A different ברייתא says the property goes back to the giver's heirs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes another ברייתא about the same case that says the property goes back to the giver's heirs. This seems to contradict the first ברייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: But isn't it taught in a ברייתא: the property goes back to the heirs of the giver!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא that rules the opposite way, which seems to undercut ריש לקיש's answer of 'אחריך שאני'. How the two sources fit together is resolved on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ברייתא said that when the second dies first, the property goes to the first person's heirs. This ברייתא says it goes to the giver's heirs. The second ruling seems to say the first person never owned the field itself, even with the wording 'after you,' so the two sources clash.

keyTerms.meaning: 'But isn't it taught in a ברייתא', used to bring a contradicting source
'They shall return', meaning the property goes back

phrases.english: But isn't it taught in a baraita:
the property goes back to the heirs of the giver!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא that contradicts the ruling discussed in steps 10 and 11
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling of the first ברייתא, as explained by 'אחריך שאני', that the property goes to the first person's heirs
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A second ברייתא on the same case gives the property to the giver's heirs, so the two ברייתות seem to contradict each other.
